subtopic_detail: Anti-D immunoglobulin dose for a sensitising event falling just beyond the twelve week threshold
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 27 year old woman in her first pregnancy at 13 weeks and 2 days. She reports fresh vaginal bleeding that soaked one pad over the past four hours, with no pain and no tissue passed.

Her booking bloods show blood group O RhD negative with a negative red cell antibody screen. A bedside ultrasound shows a single intrauterine pregnancy with foetal cardiac activity and a crown rump length consistent with dates, and no retroplacental clot. Her cervix is closed on speculum examination with a small amount of blood in the vault. She has had no previous pregnancy and has never received a blood transfusion.

data_table.Examination: Uterus non tender, cervix closed, small volume fresh blood in the posterior fornix
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O RhD negative, red cell antibody screen negative, haemoglobin 124 g/L (115-155), ultrasound showing a viable single intrauterine pregnancy at 13 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her rhesus status?

options.text: Withhold anti-D immunoglobulin now and rely on the routine prophylactic dose scheduled at twenty eight weeks
options.rationale: Routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks covers silent foetomaternal transfusion, but it does not retrospectively cover a recognised sensitising event fifteen weeks earlier. Event based and routine prophylaxis are additive, not alternatives. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

options.text: Give 250 international units of anti-D immunoglobulin intramuscularly within seventy two hours of the bleeding starting
options.rationale: The 250 international unit dose covers sensitising events before 12 completed weeks, such as miscarriage, termination or ectopic pregnancy managed in the first trimester. At 13 weeks that dose may be insufficient for the foetomaternal bleed possible at this placental mass. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

options.text: Withhold anti-D immunoglobulin and repeat the red cell antibody screen in four weeks to look for sensitisation
options.rationale: Waiting to detect anti-D antibodies means waiting for the sensitisation that prophylaxis exists to prevent, and once alloimmunisation occurs it cannot be reversed for this or any future pregnancy. Antibody screening is surveillance, not prophylaxis. (Source: National Blood Authority: Anti-D guidelines)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Anti-D guidelines

options.text: Give 625 international units of anti-D immunoglobulin intramuscularly within seventy two hours of the bleeding starting
options.rationale: Vaginal bleeding after 12 weeks is a sensitising event, and the Australian dose changes at that gestation because the volume of foetal red cells in the circulation rises with placental mass. From 12 weeks onward the dose is 625 international units, given as soon as possible and within seventy two hours. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

options.text: Perform a Kleihauer test first and give anti-D immunoglobulin only if a foetal bleed is quantified
options.rationale: Quantification of foetomaternal haemorrhage is used from 20 weeks to decide whether additional doses beyond the standard one are needed, not to decide whether to treat at all. Delaying the dose while awaiting the result risks breaching the seventy two hour window. (Source: National Blood Authority: Anti-D guidelines)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Anti-D guidelines

explanation.summary: RhD negative women who have not already formed anti-D antibodies need immunoglobulin after any potentially sensitising event so that foetal red cells entering the maternal circulation are cleared before an immune response develops. The Australian dose is gestation dependent: 250 international units before 12 completed weeks and 625 international units from 12 weeks onward, reflecting the larger possible foetomaternal bleed as the placenta grows. The dose should be given within seventy two hours, and giving it late is better than not giving it at all. Kleihauer or flow cytometry quantification is added from 20 weeks to identify the minority of women who need more than one dose. Event based prophylaxis does not replace the routine doses at 28 and 34 weeks.
key_points: Sensitising events before 12 completed weeks attract 250 international units
From 12 weeks onward the dose is 625 international units
Give within seventy two hours of the event, and still give it if late
Quantify foetomaternal haemorrhage from 20 weeks to detect the need for extra doses
Event based doses are additional to routine prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks
explanation.pearls: Check the antibody screen result before ordering anti-D, because a woman who already has immune anti-D gains nothing from prophylaxis and instead needs referral for titres and middle cerebral artery Doppler surveillance; passively acquired anti-D from a dose given within the last twelve weeks usually titres at 4 or less and should not be mistaken for immune sensitisation.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

subtopic_detail: Timing of glucose reassessment after insulin treated gestational diabetes once the baby is born
stem:
You are the obstetric resident doing a day two postnatal round on a 33 year old woman who had a normal vaginal birth at 39 weeks. She was diagnosed with gestational diabetes at 26 weeks and required isophane insulin at night from 31 weeks for fasting readings above target.

Her insulin was ceased after birth and her capillary glucose readings since delivery have all been between 4.4 and 6.1 mmol/L while eating normally. She is breastfeeding without difficulty and the baby's blood glucose screening was normal. She asks what happens next with her diabetes and whether she should stay on a monitor at home.

data_table.Examination: Uterus well contracted, lochia normal, no calf tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 4.4 to 6.1 mmol/L off insulin, booking body mass index 29 kg/m2, antenatal 75 g oral glucose tolerance test fasting 5.4 mmol/L and two hour 9.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for reassessing her glucose tolerance?

options.text: Arrange a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test before discharge from hospital, then ongoing testing every one to three years
options.rationale: Testing in the first days after birth measures a rapidly changing physiological state as placental hormones fall, so results neither confirm nor exclude persisting diabetes. The reclassification window deliberately waits for that transition to finish. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes

options.text: Arrange a fasting venous glucose level at six to twelve weeks after the birth, then ongoing testing every one to three years
options.rationale: A fasting sample alone is the least sensitive option after gestational diabetes, because post load hyperglycaemia commonly persists while fasting values normalise. Using it as the reclassification test underdiagnoses impaired glucose tolerance. (Source: RACGP: Management of type 2 diabetes)
source_refs: RACGP: Management of type 2 diabetes

options.text: Continue home capillary glucose monitoring for six weeks and arrange further testing only if readings exceed target
options.rationale: Self monitoring after birth is not a diagnostic pathway and produces scattered postprandial values that cannot be mapped onto diagnostic thresholds. Women whose home readings look acceptable still turn out to have impaired glucose tolerance on formal testing. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes

options.text: Arrange a glycated haemoglobin level at six to twelve weeks after the birth, then ongoing testing every one to three years
options.rationale: Glycated haemoglobin reflects the preceding two to three months, which in this window still includes the pregnancy itself and is further distorted by delivery related blood loss and red cell turnover. It is a reasonable interval test later, not the reclassification test. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes

options.text: Arrange a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at six to twelve weeks after the birth, then ongoing testing every one to three years
options.rationale: Postnatal reclassification uses a full oral glucose tolerance test at six to twelve weeks, once the insulin resistance of pregnancy has resolved, because a proportion of women have persistent diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance that fasting testing alone misses. Lifelong periodic screening follows because the risk of type 2 diabetes remains elevated. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes

explanation.summary: Gestational diabetes identifies a woman whose pancreatic reserve was unable to meet the insulin resistance of late pregnancy, and roughly half go on to develop type 2 diabetes within a decade. Insulin is stopped at delivery because that resistance disappears with the placenta, but the underlying tendency does not. The Australian pathway is a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at six to twelve weeks postpartum, which is early enough that women are still engaged with maternity services and late enough that the physiology has settled. Women who test normal then need repeat screening every one to three years, and sooner if they are planning another pregnancy. Needing insulin antenatally, as here, marks a higher risk group in whom the follow up test is most often abnormal.
key_points: Stop insulin at delivery; the insulin resistance of pregnancy resolves with the placenta
Reclassify with a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at six to twelve weeks postpartum
Fasting glucose and glycated haemoglobin are less sensitive in this window
Repeat screening every one to three years lifelong after a normal result
Test before any subsequent pregnancy, not just at the next booking visit
explanation.pearls: Write the six to twelve week oral glucose tolerance test request before she leaves the ward and copy it to her general practitioner, because completion rates in Australia sit near half and the commonest reason given is that nobody handed over the test; a woman who needed insulin antenatally has roughly a one in five chance of an abnormal result at that first visit.

sources.label: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes

subtopic_detail: Referral pathway when a self collected screening sample returns the higher risk oncogenic genotypes
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing results for a 41 year old woman who has never attended for cervical screening and who chose a self collected vaginal sample at her last visit. She has no abnormal bleeding, no discharge and no pain, and she has two children born vaginally.

Her sample returns positive for human papillomavirus type 16. The laboratory comment notes that liquid based cytology was not performed on this specimen. She is not pregnant, her last menstrual period was two weeks ago, and she has no immunosuppression and no history of a previous abnormal result.

data_table.Examination: Abdominal examination normal, no speculum examination performed at the screening visit
data_table.Investigations: Self collected vaginal sample positive for oncogenic human papillomavirus type 16, no cytology performed on the specimen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the human papillomavirus test in twelve months and refer for colposcopy if the same genotype persists
options.rationale: Twelve month repeat testing applies to intermediate risk results, meaning oncogenic types other than 16 and 18 with negative or low grade cytology. Applying it to type 16 leaves prevalent high grade disease untreated for a year. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines

options.text: Refer her directly for colposcopy at this visit, without taking any further sample beforehand
options.rationale: Detection of type 16 or 18 carries a high enough risk of high grade disease that referral is immediate regardless of cytology, and a self collected sample cannot be used for cytology because it does not sample the transformation zone. Adding a clinician collected test first only delays the colposcopy that is already indicated. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines

options.text: Repeat the self collected sample now to confirm the genotype before making any referral for colposcopy
options.rationale: Self collected polymerase chain reaction testing performs equivalently to clinician collection for detecting oncogenic human papillomavirus, so a confirmatory repeat adds no information. Treating the first positive as provisional is a common reason these women are lost to follow up. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines

options.text: Take a clinician collected sample for cytology and refer for colposcopy only if it shows a high grade change
options.rationale: This is the pathway for oncogenic types other than 16 and 18 found on a self collected sample, where cytology triages who needs colposcopy. With type 16 the referral threshold is already met and cytology cannot lower it. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines

options.text: Offer human papillomavirus vaccination now and rescreen in five years in line with the routine interval
options.rationale: Vaccination does not clear an established infection or treat existing disease, and returning her to the routine interval ignores a result that already meets the referral threshold. Vaccination is a separate conversation after the colposcopy pathway is under way. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Human papillomavirus)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Human papillomavirus

explanation.summary: The renewed Australian program screens primarily for oncogenic human papillomavirus, with management determined by genotype and, where available, reflex cytology. Types 16 and 18 account for most cervical cancer and carry a substantially higher immediate risk of high grade disease than the other oncogenic types, so their detection means direct colposcopy referral whatever the cytology shows. Self collection was extended to all screening participants to reach under screened and never screened women, who make up the majority of cervical cancer cases in Australia. A self collected vaginal sample is valid for the human papillomavirus test but cannot yield useful cytology, which is why type 16 or 18 on such a sample goes straight to colposcopy while other oncogenic types require a clinician collected sample for triage.
key_points: Types 16 and 18 trigger direct colposcopy referral irrespective of cytology
Other oncogenic types on a self collected sample need clinician collected cytology to triage
Self collection is not valid for cytology because it misses the transformation zone
Never screened and under screened women account for most cervical cancers in Australia
Vaccination does not alter management of an existing positive result
explanation.pearls: When a never screened woman accepts self collection, book the colposcopy or the follow up sample during the same consultation rather than waiting for the result to arrive, because the group most likely to accept self collection is also the group most likely to be lost between a positive result and the referral that follows it.

sources.label: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Choice of latency antibiotic after membranes rupture in the early third trimester
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar admitting a 29 year old woman in her second pregnancy at 30 weeks and 1 day. She reports a sudden gush of clear fluid two hours ago followed by continuing dampness, and she has no contractions and no bleeding.

Speculum examination shows a pool of clear liquor in the posterior fornix with a closed cervix. Her temperature is 36.8 degrees Celsius, the uterus is soft and non tender, and cardiotocography shows a baseline of 145 beats per minute with normal variability and no decelerations. Her low vaginal swab from 28 weeks grew no group B streptococcus. She has no penicillin allergy. The first dose of betamethasone has been given.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 145 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Clear liquor pooling in the posterior fornix, cervix closed and uneffaced, uterus soft and non tender
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5), low vaginal swab at 28 weeks negative for group B streptococcus

lead_in: Which antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Oral erythromycin given for ten days, with expectant management and daily surveillance
options.rationale: Erythromycin prolongs the interval to delivery, reduces neonatal infection and reduces the need for surfactant without the bowel injury seen with clavulanate containing regimens. Ten days, or until labour begins if sooner, is the standard course. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin in labour only, with no antibiotic while she remains undelivered
options.rationale: Intrapartum penicillin addresses group B streptococcal transmission at birth but does nothing for the ascending infection that shortens latency after membranes rupture. It is given in addition to the latency course when labour starts, not instead of it. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

options.text: No antibiotic now, with cultures repeated in forty eight hours and treatment if they are positive
options.rationale: Withholding antibiotics forfeits a proven reduction in neonatal morbidity, and surveillance cultures identify colonisation rather than the subclinical chorioamnionitis that drives preterm labour here. The benefit of the latency course does not depend on a positive culture. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Oral metronidazole given for seven days, with expectant management and daily surveillance
options.rationale: Metronidazole targets anaerobes and bacterial vaginosis organisms but has not been shown to prolong latency or improve neonatal outcomes in this setting. It is not part of the standard regimen when membranes rupture preterm. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Oral amoxicillin with clavulanic acid for ten days, with expectant management and daily surveillance
options.rationale: This combination prolonged latency but was associated with a significantly higher rate of necrotising enterocolitis in the neonates, which is why it is specifically avoided in preterm prelabour rupture of membranes. The harm outweighed the latency benefit. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

explanation.summary: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes precedes about a third of preterm births and exposes the foetus to ascending infection from the moment the barrier is lost. Antibiotics given for latency prolong the interval to delivery, reduce chorioamnionitis and reduce neonatal infection and surfactant requirement. Erythromycin is the agent of choice because the large randomised comparison found amoxicillin with clavulanic acid raised necrotising enterocolitis rates despite similar latency benefit. The course runs ten days or until labour establishes. Corticosteroids are given for lung maturity, magnesium sulfate is added for neuroprotection if birth before 30 weeks is imminent, and surveillance for chorioamnionitis by maternal observations, foetal heart rate and inflammatory markers continues throughout.
key_points: Erythromycin for ten days or until labour is the latency antibiotic of choice
Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid is avoided because of neonatal necrotising enterocolitis
Intrapartum group B streptococcal prophylaxis is additional, not a substitute
Corticosteroids for lung maturity and magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection before 30 weeks
Monitor for chorioamnionitis with observations, cardiotocography and inflammatory markers
explanation.pearls: A rising baseline foetal heart rate is often the earliest sign of chorioamnionitis and precedes maternal fever, so a baseline that has climbed from 145 to above 160 beats per minute between daily traces should prompt review for delivery even when the temperature and C reactive protein are still normal.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes
RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Choosing emergency contraception at day five when body weight reduces oral efficacy
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 24 year old woman who had unprotected intercourse five days ago, on day 11 of a regular 28 day cycle. She has taken no contraception for the past year and does not wish to be pregnant.

She weighs 96 kg with a body mass index of 34 kg/m2. She has no pelvic pain, no abnormal discharge and no history of pelvic inflammatory disease, and a urine pregnancy test today is negative. She tells you she would like reliable ongoing contraception as well, and she is willing to consider any option including a procedure today.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non tender, no cervical motion tenderness, uterus normal size and mobile
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, body mass index 34 kg/m2, last menstrual period eleven days ago

options.text: Insertion of a levonorgestrel intrauterine device today, with screening swabs taken at the same visit
options.rationale: The hormonal device does not reliably prevent implantation after intercourse has already occurred, so it is not an emergency method despite being excellent ongoing contraception. It can be placed once this cycle is shown not to be a pregnancy. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.text: Insertion of a copper intrauterine device today, with screening swabs taken at the same visit
options.rationale: The copper device remains effective up to five days after intercourse, is far more effective than any oral option, and its performance is unaffected by body weight. It also provides the ongoing contraception she is asking for, and swabs are taken at insertion rather than waiting for results. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.text: A single oral dose of levonorgestrel today, with a contraceptive discussion at a follow up visit
options.rationale: Levonorgestrel is licensed only to seventy two hours and its efficacy declines above about 70 kg, so at five days and at this weight it offers little protection. Doubling the dose is sometimes used but the evidence for that practice is weak. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: No emergency contraception because five days have elapsed, with a pregnancy test arranged in three weeks
options.rationale: Day five is within the window for the copper device, and intercourse on cycle day 11 sits squarely in the fertile period so the risk is real. Declining to act converts a preventable exposure into a wait and see. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.text: A single oral dose of ulipristal acetate today, with a contraceptive discussion at a follow up visit
options.rationale: Ulipristal is licensed to five days and outperforms levonorgestrel, but its efficacy falls with increasing body weight and it is substantially less effective than a copper device at this point in the cycle. It also delays rather than provides ongoing contraception. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

explanation.summary: Emergency contraception choice turns on three variables: time since intercourse, where the woman is in her cycle, and her body weight. The copper intrauterine device is the most effective option by a wide margin, with a failure rate below one in a thousand, and it works up to five days after intercourse or up to five days after the earliest estimated ovulation. Oral methods act by delaying ovulation, so they fail if the luteinising hormone surge has already begun, and both levonorgestrel and ulipristal lose efficacy as body weight rises. Ulipristal is licensed to five days and levonorgestrel to three. A woman who accepts a device gains both the emergency effect and long acting contraception in a single visit, which is why it is offered first rather than mentioned as an alternative.
key_points: Copper device is effective to five days and is unaffected by body weight
Levonorgestrel is licensed to seventy two hours and weakens above about 70 kg
Ulipristal is licensed to five days but efficacy also falls with rising weight
Oral methods work by delaying ovulation and fail once the surge has started
The hormonal intrauterine device is not an emergency method
explanation.pearls: Ulipristal blocks progesterone receptors, so starting a progestogen contraceptive within five days of taking it reduces its effect and can also reduce the contraceptive cover of the pill being started; if a woman takes ulipristal and wants to begin an oral contraceptive, wait five days and use condoms in between.

sources.label: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines
